messages.subject: D-RUG Map/Walk Tutorial Thursday Oct 26 10-12 Session
parts:
Hello D-RUG, 

I'm going to attempt a tutorial on two key families of functions from the purrr package during this Thursday's meeting. 

map() and walk() and their derivatives are functional programming tools that are part of the tidyverse set of packages. 

In order for you to get the most out of this tutorial I have produced an R markdown document that will let you follow along with all of the functions and examples that I will present. This document uses functions that transverse the tidyverse and therefore I would ask that if you plan to follow along on your computer that you install the tidyverse. 

install.packages("tidyverse")

I plan to roughly cover the following:
  • Data types in R
  • Functions in R
  • Iteration in R (for loops)
  • map()
  • walk()
My hope is that this isn't over anyone's head, but if there is someone out there who is familiar with the tidyverse and could help with side questions or looks of confusion that would be fantastic. 

I'm still working on the presentation, but if you're keen to look over what I've done the materials are on Github here:
https://github.com/bhive01/20171023mapwalkDRUG

The main documents are the two RmD documents:
Presentation
https://github.com/bhive01/20171023mapwalkDRUG/blob/master/20171023_DRUG_map_walk.Rmd
Coding Notebook
https://github.com/bhive01/20171023mapwalkDRUG/blob/master/purrralongwithme.Rmd

Thanks, 
Brandon

messages.author: 27405c4b711a1080
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: D-RUG Map/Walk Tutorial Thursday Oct 26 10-12 Session
parts:
D-RUG, 

As a followup, I asked about why you would use map() versus walk() on Twitter and got a couple of responses. To summarize, you can use print within map() to emulate a walk(), but one benefit of a walk() is that you get the input (.x or .) back afterwards. 
https://twitter.com/bhive01/status/923958282967908352
Quite a few responses, but as I mentioned, I've not been able to realize this benefit in a meaningful way, but that is likely due to inexperience than anything else. The proposal I haven't made is to improve the documentation so that the examples showcase this benefit better. 

Additionally, there was some question around why purrr::map() versus base::lapply() during the early parts. I hope I explained that they are effectually similar, but that due a few features and the wider family of map() functions map() was more consistent. If that wasn't clear, Hadley posted a thorough response to that exact question on SO detailing the benefits and costs of map. 
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45101045/why-use-purrrmap-instead-of-lapply/47123420#47123420

I hope that is helpful,

Brandon
